evidence.claim: An old toll-road corridor through a landscape of water supply
evidence.quote: Route 58 passes by two reservoirs (Hemlock Reservoir and Aspetuck Reservoir) that supply the Greater Bridgeport area with much of its drinking water.

evidence.claim: Route 58 follows Black Rock Turnpike north through Easton, passing Hemlock and Aspetuck reservoirs, which supply much of Greater Bridgeport’s drinking water.
evidence.quote: Route 58 passes by two reservoirs (Hemlock Reservoir and Aspetuck Reservoir) that supply the Greater Bridgeport area with much of its drinking water.

evidence.claim: A 3.1-mile section near Hemlock Reservoir is a designated scenic highway.
evidence.quote: A 3.1-mile (5.0 km) section in Easton near the Hemlock Reservoir is a designated scenic highway.

evidence.claim: The surrounding town developed slowly among rough hills along the Aspetuck River.
evidence.quote: The area was slow to develop because of the rough hills along the Aspetuck River

evidence.claim: The turnpike name joins two separate road ventures.
evidence.quote: Both turnpike roads are collectively known as Black Rock Turnpike today.

evidence.claim: In 1797, the Fairfield, Weston, and Redding Turnpike was chartered to improve the route north from Easton village through Redding Ridge into Bethel.
evidence.quote: In May 1797, the northern portion of Redding Road was chartered as the Fairfield, Weston, and Redding Turnpike. The turnpike company improved the road from Easton village through Redding Ridge into Bethel

evidence.claim: In 1832, the road from Black Rock harbor to Easton village became a public toll road.
evidence.quote: In May 1832, the road from Black Rock harbor to Easton village was chartered as a public toll road

evidence.claim: The modern Route 58 number dates to the 1932 state highway renumbering.
evidence.quote: Modern Route 58 was created in the 1932 state highway renumbering from old Highway 124.

evidence.claim: Travel north from Fairfield into Easton along Black Rock Turnpike, also called Black Rock Road within Easton.
evidence.quote: Route 58 continues northward along the Black Rock Turnpike, passing through the towns of Easton and Redding.

evidence.claim: Hemlock Reservoir’s dam was completed in 1914; the reservoir supplies water to Fairfield, Bridgeport and nearby towns.
evidence.quote: Its completion was marked by the creation of the Hemlock Reservoir Dam, which was completed in 1914, and provides water to Fairfield, Bridgeport, and several other nearby towns.

evidence.claim: Its connections extend beyond the water beside the road: an underground aqueduct carries diverted water from Saugatuck Reservoir to Aspetuck Reservoir.
evidence.quote: The Aspetuck Reservoir is fed water diverted from the Saugatuck Reservoir via an underground aqueduct.

evidence.claim: Water is also diverted from Aspetuck into Hemlock, which then flows into the Mill River.
evidence.quote: Water from the Aspetuck Reservoir is also diverted into the Hemlock Reservoir in Easton and Fairfield, which then flows into the Mill River.

evidence.claim: On April 25, 1777, British troops under General William Tryon marched toward Danbury to destroy homes, warehouses and ammunition stores.
evidence.quote: On April 25, 1777, during the Revolutionary War, British soldiers under the command of General William Tryon marched up the Redding Road

evidence.claim: They used Redding Road, which paralleled present Route 58 south of Easton center and followed its alignment north of the center.
evidence.quote: which paralleled present-day Route 58 south of Easton center and ran along Route 58 north of Easton center

evidence.claim: The northern road became a chartered turnpike twenty years later, carrying the names Fairfield, Weston and Redding.
evidence.quote: In May 1797, the northern portion of Redding Road was chartered as the Fairfield, Weston, and Redding Turnpike.

evidence.claim: to destroy homes, warehouses and ammunition stores.
evidence.quote: on their way to Danbury to destroy homes, warehouses and ammunition stores as part of the Danbury Raid.

evidence.claim: The Bradley-Hubbell House overlooks a reservoir that swallowed much of its farmland.
evidence.quote: In 1912, Bradley descendants sold the property to the Bridgeport Hydraulic Company, which flooded much of the farmland for a reservoir

evidence.claim: Built in 1816 for Aljah and Elizabeth Bradley, the house has a traditional central chimney and Federal-style details, including oval windows in the gables.
evidence.quote: Built in 1816 for Aljah and Elizabeth Bradley, it is a Colonial with a traditional center-chimney plan and a few Federal-style ornaments, including oval windows in the gables

evidence.claim: The family sold the property to Bridgeport Hydraulic Company in 1912; the company leased the house to its employee Franklin Hubbell.
evidence.quote: In 1912, Bradley descendants sold the property to the Bridgeport Hydraulic Company, which flooded much of the farmland for a reservoir and leased the house to Franklin Hubbell

evidence.claim: The house was donated to the Easton Historical Society in 1998.
evidence.quote: In 1998, the house was donated to the Easton Historical Society

evidence.claim: At 535 Black Rock Turnpike, its view is over Aspetuck Reservoir.
evidence.quote: The Bradley-Hubbell House is an historic house located at 535 Black Rock Turnpike in Easton, Connecticut.

flags: No saved agency or tourism account explains the scenic designation, and 00.txt provides no curves, grades, viewpoints or travel time. Intro stays shorter rather than inventing driving detail. Exact Fairfield-line/Freeborn-Road designation boundaries appear only in material, so are omitted.

Hemlock and Redding Road moments remain short because relevant evidence is limited. Current reservoir fish species and fishing prohibition are supported by 01.txt but omitted as peripheral, unverified visitor logistics; no fishing is encouraged.

Dropped current tagline’s water-company woods claim: cached ownership does not establish woodland on this section. The townwide half-owned claim is supported but not used as a roadside land-cover description.
Redding Road is retained as an unpinned corridor-history moment, not a verified stopping place. New Bradley-Hubbell House coordinates come from 08.txt; no interior access is promised.

02.txt opens its history with the apparent error “New York was first settled in 1757”; did not use that claim. 08.txt spells the reservoir “Aspectuck”; standardized to Aspetuck as in 00.txt and 07.txt.
